content.thinking:
I'm piecing together the timeline: account pages started failing at 00:36, with the payment provider returning 503s on the card endpoint 14 times between 00:36–00:42, and account page errors peaking at 00:37. Since there were no deploys or flag changes, this points to the provider's outage as the root cause rather than anything on our side.

These are absence-of-change facts, so they belong in the ruled_out list for the step tying the incident to what triggered it — the provider starting to 503 at 00:36. The mechanism itself is supported directly by Gbf7d, which shows the account page request failing with PaymentProviderFailed when the provider call errors; the "no fallback by design" detail from F1 just adds context but the core causal link is the observed log failure.

I'm leaning toward keeping the root cause tied to what Gbf7d actually shows: the account page calls io-pay for the shopper's card on every request and fails the request when that call doesn't return successfully, and the provider began returning 503s at onset. The reason behind the provider's 503s isn't established in the record, and I need to check whether "every request" is actually substantiated by the near-100% error rate.

The chain builds as symptom (account pages failing per Gbac1/Gbf7d) leading to cause (card endpoint returning 503, raising PaymentProviderFailed, with deploy and flags ruled out) leading to mechanism (page can't render without the card, so it fails whenever the lookup fails). I'll stop there since why io-pay itself returned 503 isn't shown in the evidence.

3. Step three answers why the 503 on the card lookup failed the page: the account page has no retry or fallback when the card lookup fails, per the code Code-Fix read, citing Gbf7d and F1. I should stop there since why io-pay itself returned 503 isn't shown in the evidence, and I'm second-guessing whether this mechanism needs more support beyond the G rows already citing it.

I'll settle on a root cause tied to Gbf7d: the account page needs the shopper's card from io-pay to render and fails the request when the provider doesn't return it, and io-pay's card endpoint answered 503, so account page requests failed — why io-pay returned 503 isn't in the record. No earlier changes need to be ruled out since none were found. The ClientDisconnected errors in G46bc from 00:06–00:35 look like pre-onset baseline noise that stopped before the issue window, alongside Gad41's normal render at 00:13, so I may note those as ruled-out noise rather than causal.

For contributing factors, I'm considering that nobody was paged for the alert, meaning no on-call incident was linked, so someone would've contacted io-pay sooner had paging worked — this factor held before the incident. I'm also weighing whether the account page's lack of a degraded mode for card-provider failures counts as a separate contributing factor, since it's a hard dependency on a third party, but I worry this overlaps with the root cause itself rather than being distinct, so I may need to phrase it differently or skip it.

I'm also thinking about whether there's no direct monitor on io-pay's own availability — the issue was only caught via io-shop's error-rate alert — and whether a dependency probe would've sped up detection, though it seems marginal. A stronger candidate might be the absence of an established escalation path or runbook for contacting IO Payments Ltd directly, since the incident only reached a human after escalation rather than through an automated contact route.

Now I'm drafting action items: page an on-call rotation off the HighErrorRate alert for CF-1, ask IO Payments Ltd to restore the endpoint and explain the 503s as a mitigation step, write a vendor escalation runbook for io-pay outages to address CF-2, and add a dedicated alert on io-pay 503 rates so provider outages get named explicitly for CF-3.

For lessons learned, I'm noting what went well — the investigator correctly traced onset to io-pay 503s and ruled out io-shop deploys/flags as causes, and Code-Fix appropriately held back since the design wasn't actually broken. For what went wrong, I'm weighing whether "nobody was paged" belongs here as its own finding, separate from being a contributing factor.

I'm also drafting the went_wrong entry noting that no outreach to IO Payments was recorded by the time the incident escalated, and confirming there's nothing to add for got_lucky or still_at_risk beyond the ongoing exposure to future io-pay outages. I'm starting to phrase the symptom and cause statements now.

The chain does reach a cause: the provider's failures triggered the breakage since the account page depends on the card data. I should flag assumptions too — that all account page failures during this window trace to the same provider issue, and that the running revision stayed constant across replicas with no deploys in between.

action_items.item: Ask IO Payments Ltd to restore the io-pay card endpoint, and to explain why it answered with errors.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
Write a runbook for io-pay outages, with the IO Payments Ltd support contact, status page and escalation route.
Add an alert on the share of io-shop's calls to io-pay that fail, so that a provider outage is named as one when it is detected.
Have the account page's product owner decide whether, during provider outages, the page should show with a 'card unavailable' notice instead of failing.

causal_chain.step: From the onset, shoppers asking for their account page got a failed page instead of the page itself.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release of io-shop: no production change came back for the day before the onset, and all replicas ran a single revision.
A feature flag change: the flag provider showed no flag changes by anyone but Argus in the hour before it was read.
Shoppers closing the connection (ClientDisconnected) as the cause: those errors were logged only before the onset, and stopped before the provider failures began.

causal_chain.step: Each failing request failed at the card lookup: io-pay (api.io-pay.example, run by IO Payments Ltd) answered {Gbf7d.1} when asked for the shopper's card, and io-shop raised PaymentProviderFailed and returned a failed page. These failures began in the onset minute and went on through the last minute read.
The account page cannot be served without the shopper's card, so a failed card lookup fails the whole page.

input.cause_in_plain_words: The outside company that supplies shoppers' saved card details stopped returning them, and the shop's account page cannot be shown without those details, so the page failed.

contributing_factors.factor: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been working on the outage as soon as the alert fired, and could have contacted IO Payments Ltd to get the card endpoint restored, rather than the incident only reaching a human once Argus escalated it.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No runbook or escalation path to IO Payments Ltd for io-pay outages was seen in the record. Nothing Argus could do reached the provider.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Asking the provider to restore the endpoint could have started straight away from a known contact, which could have shortened the outage.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No alert on io-pay's own availability, or on io-shop's failed calls to it, was seen. The outage was found only by io-shop's overall error-rate alert.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The alert would have named the failing provider directly, so the people responding would have known at once that the fix lay with IO Payments Ltd.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent checked deploys, releases, flags, logs and the service register, and pinned the failure on io-pay's card endpoint in its candidate C1.
Argus read the flag provider's history and found no flag changes by anyone else, which ruled out a flag change on io-shop's side.
Argus declined to act on C1, because the failure was in a service another company runs and nothing Argus could do would reach it.
The Code-Fix Agent read the provider and account page code and their tests. It proposed no change and left a product decision to people.

went_wrong: By the time the incident was escalated, the record shows no request sent to IO Payments Ltd to restore the card endpoint.

input.root_cause: io-shop's account page fetches the shopper's saved card from the third-party provider io-pay on each request and fails the whole request when the provider does not return the card. Once io-pay's card endpoint began answering {Gbf7d.1}, account page requests failed with PaymentProviderFailed. The record does not show why io-pay returned {Gbf7d.1}.
input.still_at_risk: Account pages could go on failing for as long as io-pay's card endpoint keeps answering with errors, and any later outage at io-pay would fail them again in the same way.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
